The key fact here is that security groups and NACLs drop traffic silently — they never send back an RST or RST,ACK. So if tshark is showing an RST,ACK coming back from the destination, that means the packet already reached 10.0.4.40 and the host itself refused the connection, likely because nothing's listening on port 8080 or a local firewall is rejecting it. That tells me opening the security group won't fix anything, since the SG/NACL layer is already letting the traffic through — the problem lives on the host.

{"id": "77a136a5-8f7f-424a-ae1c-dc5c7806f6e6", "role": "assistant", "content": [{"text": "No — opening the security group won't fix this, and here's why.

**Answer:** SGs and NACLs drop non-matching traffic silently; they never generate a reply packet. A RST,ACK coming back *from* 10.0.4.40 means your SYN already reached that host and its TCP stack actively refused the connection — almost always because nothing is listening on port 8080 there (or a host firewall explicitly rejected it). The security group is already letting this traffic through.

**Evidence label:** Inferred — follows from documented AWS/TCP behavior (SG/NACL = silent drop; RST = response from a host, firewall, or router), not something I verified against your actual capture bytes.

**Read-only check to confirm:** On the box behind 10.0.4.40, check what's bound to 8080 (e.g. `sudo ss -ltnp | grep 8080`). From your side, you can also sanity-check the SG allows it without changing anything: `aws ec2 describe-security-groups --filters Name=ip-permission.to-port,Values=8080` against the ENI/instance owning 10.0.4.40.

**Coverage gap:** I'm going on your description, not the actual tshark output — if you paste the handshake lines (SYN → SYN,RST or RST,ACK with ports/seq) I can confirm the capture point and rule out a middlebox sending the reset instead of the host itself.", "type": "text"}], "created_at": null}
